case.title: Around the Bend
case.hook: Good news! Mr. Ortiz took our advice. This year’s Duck Derby will float down Palmetto Creek, where the water flows. But the creek bends the long way around a marsh, and the practice run went wrong.

map.duckWord: 🦆 the ducks float the long way
map.alt: Mr. Ortiz’s hand-drawn map. Palmetto Creek bends the long way around an open marsh, past a little waterfall. The start dock and the finish dock are 300 feet apart across the marsh.

creek.mapCap: Mr. Ortiz’s map. The judges can see each other across the marsh, 300 feet apart.

log.head: WALKIE-TALKIE PRACTICE RUN
log.sub: Saturday, 6:55 p.m. · Start dock and finish dock
rows: The ducks are here, and there’s no net!

body: Our walkie-talkies cut out at the bend, and the waterfall drowns out shouting.
Race night starts at 6:30 p.m., just before sunset. The judges need a code they can flash across the marsh: READY, WAIT, GO and WINNER IN. Can you help us make one that won’t get mixed up?

case.question: What code should the judges use on race night, and how will they know it works?
case.how: Find 4 clues as you work through the lesson. Then crack the case (solve it) at the top of the Assignment tab.

clues.t: The knock meant nothing until the code key came out. A pattern is a code only when the sender and the receiver share the same rules.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 1: the flashlight key
clues.t: A good code uses patterns that are easy to tell apart, like clearly short and clearly long flashes. A flash in between got a “?”.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 2: which signal crosses the bend?
clues.t: No signal, a loud waterfall, sunset and no ropes across the water: only a flashlight met every goal inside every limit.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 3: test it across the creek
clues.t: The judges’ first code failed the partner test: short flashes in a row got mixed up. After a redesign and a new test, the partner read 4 out of 4.

solve.title: Which code should the judges use?
solve.q: Which plan fits all four clues?

options.t: Talk on the walkie-talkies, but louder.
options.why: Check Clue 3. There’s no signal at the bend, and the waterfall drowns out voices.

options.t: Full Morse code for every letter. More patterns make a better code.
options.why: Check Clue 2 and Clue 4. More patterns mean more chances to mix them up. Simple codes are often best.

options.t: A simple flashlight code where every message looks very different, tested by a partner at the creek and redesigned until the partner reads 4 out of 4.
options.why: Case cracked! A code works when both judges share the key, the patterns are easy to tell apart, and a partner test proves it.

options.t: Mr. Ortiz’s first code. He can read it, so it works.
options.why: Check Clue 1 and Clue 4. The finish judge has to read it too, and the partner test mixed it up.

knock.afterText: Listen to the knock, then knock it back.
knock.title: The secret knock

why.t: A knock pattern that friends agree on, so they know who is at the door without opening it or talking.

todo: Press Listen to the knock.
Tap the door to knock the same rhythm back. Knocks close together make a group. A pause starts a new one.
Then find the code key.
knock.alt: A wooden clubhouse door with a CLUB sign and a red welcome mat.

rounds.ask: Listen first. Then knock it back.
rounds.done: You knocked it back exactly: knock-knock … knock!

rounds.ask: Now answer with the club code. Tell your friend “Come in!”
rounds.done: Your friend heard “Come in!” and opened the door.

knock.q0: You copied the knock. But what does it MEAN?
knock.q1: The code key is out! What did the first knock mean?
knock.q1Miss: Find the row with the same dots as the knock you copied.
knock.q: Why could you read the knock only after you found the key?

opts.t: A pattern becomes a code when both people know the rules

opts.miss: The knocks were the same. What did the key give you?
Anyone with the key can read it. What is written on the key?

knock.win: A pattern means something only when the sender and the receiver share the same rules. That’s a code! Clue 1!

morsekey.title: The flashlight key

why.t: A code where each letter is a pattern of short and long signals: clicks, beeps or flashes of light.

todo: Tap the red key quickly for a short flash (a dot). Hold it down for a long flash (a dash).
Stop for a moment after each letter.
Send SOS. Then send GO.

rounds.ask: SOS means “help!” Send it: three short, three long, three short.
rounds.done: You sent SOS! Ships have used this pattern to call for help.

rounds.ask: Now send GO, the start signal for the race.

morsekey.wobbly: That flash was too long for a dot and too short for a dash. Your partner can’t tell which one you meant! Tap quickly for a dot, or hold longer for a dash.
morsekey.wrongLetter: The letter {want} is {code}. Start the word again.
morsekey.q: Why does Morse code use just two kinds of flashes, short and long?

opts.t: They are easy to tell apart, so the receiver doesn’t mix them up

opts.miss: A long flash isn’t brighter. It just lasts longer. Why is that easy to read?
Anyone with the code key can read it. Think about the orange “?” on your strip.

morsekey.win: A code works when its patterns are easy to tell apart. A flash that wasn’t clearly short or long got a “?”. Clue 2!

lighthouse.title: Every lighthouse has a fingerprint

why.t: At night a sailor can’t see the tower, only its light. Each lighthouse flashes its own pattern, so sailors know which one they are looking at.

todo: Count each light’s flashes before it goes dark.
Drag each name onto its lighthouse, or tap a name and then a lighthouse.
lighthouse.alt: A model of a dark Florida coast at night with three lighthouses, A, B and C. Each one blinks its own pattern.
lighthouse.miss: Count that light’s flashes before it goes dark. {name}: {short}.

photo.alt: The real Cape Canaveral Lighthouse: a tall tower with wide black and white stripes, a lantern room on top, a palm tree and a small brick building at its base, under a blue sky.
photo.cap: The real Cape Canaveral Lighthouse in Florida. Every night it still flashes twice every 20 seconds, and sailors can see it about 24 nautical miles (28 miles) out at sea. Photo: NASA/Jim Grossmann, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

lighthouse.done: Sailors read the pattern, not the tower. Two flashes every 20 seconds means Cape Canaveral: a code made of light!

crossbend.afterText: Which signal can cross the bend?
crossbend.title: Which signal crosses the bend?
todo: Tap each limit to switch it on.
Watch which ways to send a message get crossed out.
Then check the last one against each goal.

map.alt: Mr. Ortiz’s hand-drawn map. Palmetto Creek bends the long way around an open marsh, past a little waterfall. The start dock and the finish dock are 300 feet apart across the marsh.

crossbend.limitsLabel: The limits at the bend (constraints): tap each one to switch it on

tools.t: A bell on a rope across the creek

limits.t: No signal at the bend: phones and walkie-talkies cut out
The waterfall is too loud to hear voices
The race ends at sunset, when it gets dark
limits.why: Too dark to see flags at sunset.

limits.t: Nothing can stretch across the water: the ducks float through
limits.why: A rope would catch the ducks.

crossbend.leftLine: Only one is left: {t}. Does it meet every goal?
crossbend.goalsLabel: The goals (criteria): tap each one to check

goals.t: Reaches the finish dock, 300 feet away
goals.ok: At dusk, a bright flashlight can be seen much farther than 300 feet.
Short and long flashes can make lots of different patterns.

goals.t: The finish judge can read it in a few seconds
goals.ok: A short pattern of flashes takes just a second or two.

crossbend.q: Which one of these is a CONSTRAINT (a limit)?

opts.t: The waterfall is too loud to hear voices

opts.miss: That’s a goal: something the design must DO. A constraint is a limit.
That’s a goal too. Which one limits what you can use?

crossbend.win: Criteria are the goals. Constraints are the limits. At the bend, only the flashlight met every goal inside every limit. Clue 3!

codetest.afterText: change one thing and test again.
codetest.title: Test it across the creek

why.t: Your partner writes down what they see. Here a model partner reads your flashes from the finish dock, 300 feet away.

todo: Press Test across the creek to test the judges’ first code.
Read the test sheet. Which messages got mixed up?
Change ONE thing: a pattern tile on one message, or the gap. Then test again.
Keep going until your partner reads 4 out of 4. There’s more than one way to fix it, so be creative!
codetest.tilesLabel: Pattern tiles: drag one onto a message, or tap a tile and then a message
codetest.firstLine: Test the judges’ first code before you change anything. Press Test across the creek.
codetest.oneLine: You already changed one thing. Test it first! Engineers change ONE thing at a time, so they know what fixed it.
codetest.sameLine: Nothing changed, so the test would come out the same. Change ONE thing first: a tile or the gap.
codetest.changedLine: Changes since the last test: {n} of 1
codetest.failLine: Some messages got mixed up. Those are your failure points. Change ONE thing and test again.
codetest.q: The judges’ first code failed its test. What does that tell an engineer?

opts.t: What to fix next: a failed test shows where to redesign
The code is no good, so give up
opts.miss: Engineers don’t give up. What did the test sheet show you to change?

opts.t: Real engineers never fail a test
opts.miss: Real engineers test early so they can find failures. How many tests did you run?

codetest.win: Test, find the failure points, change one thing, test again. That’s redesign, and it got the code to 4 out of 4. Clue 4!

fogtwist.title: Race night: mist on the creek
todo: Test your code once more, in the real place, on race night.
Read the mist test sheet.
If it fails, pick a fix and test again.

map.alt: Mr. Ortiz’s hand-drawn map. Palmetto Creek bends the long way around an open marsh, past a little waterfall. The start dock and the finish dock are 300 feet apart across the marsh.

fogtwist.intro: Race night, 7 p.m. As the sun sets, a thin mist rises off Palmetto Creek. In mist, a light looks fuzzy and spread out, so quick flashes can blur into one long glow.
fogtwist.testBtn: 🔦 Test my code in the mist
fogtwist.fixQ: Your code got mixed up in the mist. What ONE change would help most?

fixes.t: Make the gaps between flashes longer

fixes.miss: Remember the waterfall! Shouting can’t cross the marsh.

fixes.t: Give up: the code doesn’t work
fixes.miss: A failed test isn’t the end. It shows you what to change.
More messages means more patterns to mix up. What would make the flashes easier to count?

fogtwist.readyLine: Your long gaps were ready for the mist: 4 out of 4! Engineers still test in the real place, in real weather, to be sure.
fogtwist.passLine: Long gaps: 4 out of 4 in the mist! One more redesign, and the code is ready for race night.
fogtwist.win: Test, redesign, test again, even on race night. Engineers don’t expect to get it right the first time. They test until it works.

myname.title: Send your name in Morse code
todo: Type your first name.
Press Send it and watch the light blink each letter.
Compare the time with a one-flash race signal.
myname.onlyLetters: Type your first name with letters A to Z.
myname.compare: A one-flash race signal takes less than 1 second. Simple codes are fast!
myname.done: Now you can sign your name in light!

myname.tease: Type your name and watch it blink in Morse code.

q1.A: A computer program can use a code, but think about the knock at the clubhouse door. What turned those knocks into a message?
q1.C: Anyone with the club’s code key could read the knock. A code is the set of rules.

q2.B: Think about the partner test. After it failed, what did one change do?
q2.C: Swapping to another confusing code won’t help. What made the judges’ code work?

q3.A: “No talking” is a LIMIT on how you send. Which choice says what the code must DO?
q3.B: “Only one hand” is a limit too. Which choice is a goal?

hlCoach.title: Highlight like a scientist
tips: Highlight key words, not whole paragraphs.
If everything is yellow, nothing stands out. Aim for a few words in each paragraph.
Look for words that are explained.
Bold words, and words followed by “means”, “is called” or a meaning in ( ), are often worth saving.
Look for answers to the Big Question.
Ask yourself: does this tell how a pattern becomes a code, or how to test and fix one?
“Because”, “so” and “first … then” show how ideas connect.
Yellow = important. Green = evidence I might use in my answer. Pink = something I wonder about.

practice.q: Practice: tap the 3 to 5 words that matter most in this sentence.
practice.text: A code works only when the receiver knows the rules and can tell the patterns apart.
practice.model: A scientist might highlight “code”, “rules” and “patterns”. Those words hold the big idea.

hlCoach.outside: This works in every subject. When you read anything, save the words that answer your question, and skip the rest.
